title: The Shared Document With the Wrong Link
script: Narrator: [warmly] I prepared a volunteer schedule in an online document and sent the link to thirty people. Five minutes later, a friend warned me that anyone with the link could edit it.
Narrator: I opened the file and saw that two names had already moved to different time slots. I could not tell whether the changes were mistakes or intentional.
Narrator: [thoughtful] The schedule also contained phone numbers for team leaders. It should never have been open for public editing.
Narrator: I changed the link settings immediately. General volunteers received view access, while three coordinators received edit access through their named accounts.
Narrator: [carefully] Then I checked the version history. It showed exactly which rows had changed and allowed me to restore the correct schedule.
Narrator: I removed personal phone numbers from the main table and placed contact details in a separate restricted file.
Narrator: [reflective] I sent a new message explaining the corrected link. I did not blame the people who had opened the first one because the permission mistake was mine.
Narrator: One volunteer asked why clicking the old link no longer worked. I explained that access had been limited to protect the schedule.
Narrator: [honestly] After the event, our team created a short sharing checklist: identify the audience, choose view or edit, remove sensitive data, test the link, and set an end date.
Narrator: We also created a duplicate practice file so new coordinators could learn permissions without risking real information.
Narrator: [gently] Cloud documents feel simple because one button creates a link. That convenience can hide important choices about who may see, copy, or change data.
Narrator: A link is not automatically private just because we send it inside a group chat.
Narrator: [encouraging] Now I open a private browser window and test shared links from the receiver's view before sending them.
Narrator: The mistake lasted only a few minutes, but it taught me that access settings are part of responsible communication, not a technical detail for someone else.

quiz.question: What was wrong with the first link?
options: Anyone with it could edit the schedule
quiz.explanation: The file had overly broad editing permission.

quiz.question: What private information was exposed?
quiz.explanation: Contact numbers were inside the open file.

quiz.question: How were changes repaired?
quiz.explanation: The record showed and reversed unwanted edits.

quiz.question: What permissions were chosen?
options: View for volunteers and named editing for coordinators
quiz.explanation: Access now matches each person’s role.

quiz.question: What final habit does the narrator adopt?
options: Test links from the receiver’s view
Keep sensitive data in all files
Trust group chats as private storage
quiz.explanation: Testing reveals what another person can actually access.

quiz.question: Why can the moved names not be treated as deliberate harm?
options: The narrator cannot yet tell whether changes were mistakes or intentional

quiz.question: What does named-account editing improve?
options: Access and changes can be limited and traced to coordinators

quiz.question: Why move phone numbers to another file?
options: The main schedule has a wider audience than contact details need

quiz.question: What does testing in a private window reveal?
options: What a receiver can actually access without the owner’s session
quiz.explanation: Testing from the recipient view checks real permissions.

quiz.question: What is the narrator’s responsibility?
options: Correct the link, explain the change, and improve the system without false blame
quiz.explanation: Ownership of the setup error leads to repair.
